title: Nriga Ascends, and Krishna Warns the City
subtitle: The lizard-king's merit claims its ending
story:
The king who stood before Krishna had been a lizard an hour before — a lizard the size of a hill, at the bottom of a dry well outside Dwaraka, until Krishna drew him out and his true form returned. He was Nriga, a king of ancient days, once famed for giving away more cows than there are stars in the sky, and he had just finished telling how one mistaken gift had cost him so many years in a well. Now the words were running out, and praise was taking their place.

“What is there that you do not know, lord?” he said. “Yet I, who lay so long in blindness at the bottom of a well, have come to see you with my own eyes — you whom the wise seek in the depths of their hearts, whom the scriptures only glimpse, the lord beyond the reach of the senses. The very sight of you is the end of birth and of fear.”

Then he asked for what he had been waiting to ask. “Permit me, Krishna,” he said, “to go to the celestial world, where the merit of my giving has been waiting all these years.” He bowed, circled Krishna, and touched Krishna's feet with his head. Then he stood, and waited.

But Krishna did not send him off in silence. He turned to the citizens of Dwaraka, who had gathered to watch the wonder, and what he said to them was meant to outlast the day.

“The property of a brahmana,” Krishna said, “even a little of it, enjoyed without right, is fire that cannot be digested. I do not count the poison halahala the deadliest thing in the world, for even that has an antidote: poison kills the one who eats it, and water quenches fire. But the wealth of a brahmana, taken without leave, destroys three generations of the house that takes it.”

He went on, and his voice carried to the farthest listeners. “Kings, blinded by their royal fortune, do not see their own fall. For every handful of dust they seize, and for every tear of those they rob, they and their houses pay in years — unchecked, unrepentant, until the reckoning comes. Whoever takes the livelihood of a brahmana, whether it was given by his own hand or another's — may such wealth never come near me, for men who covet it become short-lived. And you, my people: never do harm to a brahmana, even one who has erred. As I bow to the brahmanas, attentive and well-disposed, so should you. Wealth torn from a brahmana drags the taker down.”

The words fell on the gathered citizens and settled into them. Then, while the silence was still new, a celestial car descended — bright and fragrant, shining as if it were made of the morning itself — and came to rest before Nriga.

Nriga looked at Krishna once more. Then he stepped into the car, and the car rose. It climbed above the walls of Dwaraka, above the roofs and the upturned faces, and Nriga's form grew small and bright against the sky until it was only a point of light — and then nothing.

The citizens stood looking up long after it was gone.
reflection: Krishna's warning is carefully framed: he does not exalt brahmanas as a class so much as mark how the powerful consume what they never earned, and how a single unknowing wrong, even inside a life of great charity, still exacts its price. The poison metaphor — worse than halahala, because no antidote exists — carries the whole weight of the teaching.
next_story_tease: But far from Dwaraka, in the kingdom of Karusha, a king had begun to call himself the true Vasudeva — and his claim would not go unanswered.
hero_scene: King Nriga, radiant, ascending in a celestial car above the walls of Dwaraka while Krishna stands below addressing the gathered citizens with one hand raised in teaching, the people looking up at both.
